title: Rafi and Cora's Body-Powered Climb
markdown:
Dawn laid orange and pink across the workshop roof in streaks that looked, for a moment, like somebody had set the sky on fire and then thought better of it. Rafi bounced out of bed as if the mattress had been waiting for an excuse. Today was Sunstone Peak day. His toolkit sat on the desk already packed, gadgets nested by size, and it had the air of an object that would have packed itself if he had slept five minutes longer.

Outside, Cora the jackdaw tapped the windowpane with a beak that never wasted a knock. Black feathers took the first light the way polished stone takes a polish: all at once, and as if they had meant to.

“Cora. Ready?”

“Peak. Peak.” Her head bobbed so fast it blurred. She was always ready for anything he cooked up, including the things that later required a second toolkit.

They dashed to the climbing wall behind the workshop, Cora hopping the last stretch as if the ground were a suggestion. This was the last practice before the real expedition, the one that promised a view so wide you could lose an argument in it. Rafi had already laid out carabiners in a line and named the peak under his breath, a habit that made a plan feel like a place. Then his eyes went to the top of the practice rope and stopped. The thick climbing rope, usually as dependable as a well-tied boot, looked fuzzy.

“It’s frayed. Right at the top.” He said it quietly, because loudness would not have helped the fibres. The rope was too weak to trust. The climb had become a problem with a name.

He tugged the frayed section. Threads loosened and threatened to come away entirely. Cora tilted her head and watched his arm as he tested the damage, intelligent eyes doing the work of a second pair of hands.

“What’s wrong?”

Rafi looked down at his own arm as if it had volunteered. He bent his elbow. Click: a tiny, precise movement. He felt the tight pull of the bicep. He shrugged his shoulder. Creak: a broader, more powerful shift. He twisted his wrist. Swivel: a delicate, controlled turn.

“See? The arm works because of the elbow. A joint. A pivot. This muscle here—” he flexed, and the bicep made a small hill “—pulls the arm up. This one on the back, the triceps, pushes it down. They work together. Push and pull. A team that does not need a meeting.”

Cora flapped, tucked, hopped, and spun in a circle that would have made a compass dizzy. She pointed at her own wing with a talon.

“Wing bones. Wing muscles. Flap and grip. We bend. We move. Like you.”

Rafi’s grin arrived before the plan finished dressing. “Your wings are like my arms. Bones as levers. Wing joints as pivot points. We can fix this with a knot that does not argue.”

He pounded back into the workshop, past the shelf of nearly-good gadgets, and came out with a long tough vine, flexible as a dancer and twice as stubborn. He had kept it for a repair that had not yet happened. “New anchor.”

At the wall he looped the vine around a sturdy unfrayed metal hook at the top. The first throw missed; the elbow had not yet been invited. He bent it on purpose, felt the bicep take the load, and the loop sat. He pulled one end with the biceps, then used the triceps to push the other end and cinch the loop, wrist twisting for the last precise millimetre, the whole chain of joints doing the guiding that a single stiff stick never could. “Joints put the vine where it has to be. Muscles work against each other so the knot comes tight instead of theatrical. If I only pulled, the loop would stay a shrug.”

Cora gripped with beak and talons and pulled the vine taut as he finished the cinch, her own wing joints folding and opening like a second pair of elbows. “Tight. Strong.”

Ms. Lin walked over then, the sort of mentor whose presence made a climbing wall remember its manners. Her eyes had already found the fray, the vine, and the knot.

“Trouble, climbers?”

Rafi pointed at the new anchor without puffing his chest quite as far as he wanted to. “We fixed it. The skeleton is a set of levers made of bone. Joints let them move. Muscles pull and push. That is how the knot got made, and how it stayed made.”

Ms. Lin nodded. “Bones as levers. Joints as pivots. Muscles in pairs, one contracting while the other eases, so the action is the one you meant. That control is what keeps a climb from becoming a fall. You have been using levers and joints all morning. Now you can name them.”

Rafi looked up at the vine. “So we can still go to Sunstone Peak.”

Cora ruffled. “Peak. Peak.”

They tested the knot with a slow first pull, then a second, then the kind of third pull that is really a conversation with gravity. The vine held. Rafi climbed three holds, felt the paired muscles do the same work they had done on the knot, and came down grinning at his own elbows as if they had passed an exam. Cora hopped the side-route and scolded a loose flake of bark. Ms. Lin marked the hook with chalk so tomorrow’s self would not trust last week’s rope by habit.

Rafi logged fray at top hook / vine cinch / biceps–triceps pair in the workshop book, left the old rope coiled where Ms. Lin could cut it for scrap, and let Cora inspect the new anchor as if she had personally invented elbows. The wall, ordinary wood and honest metal, waited. They climbed again, this time all the way, Sunstone Peak still a day away and no longer a rumour of a fray.
